A Mathematical Model for Butterfly Wing Patterns

Citation

Traore, E. N. (2017). A Mathematical Model for Butterfly Wing Patterns. Project report supervised by Filippo Remonato and Mats Ehrnstrøm.

Read the paper.

Overview

The report studies a mathematical model based on two interacting processes:

  1. A morphogen diffuses across the wing and degrades over time.
  2. The local morphogen concentration activates a gene product that controls later pigmentation.

The author implements the model numerically and investigates how changes in parameters, domain size, and initial morphogen placement affect the resulting wing pattern.

The Model

Morphogen Diffusion

The morphogen concentration \(S\) evolves according to

\[ \frac{\partial S}{\partial t} = D\nabla^2S - K\gamma S. \]

This equation describes two competing processes:

  • Diffusion (\(D\nabla^2S\)), which spreads morphogen across the wing.
  • Degradation (\(-K\gamma S\)), which removes morphogen over time.

Terms

  • \(S\) is the morphogen concentration.
  • \(\frac{\partial S}{\partial t}\) is the rate of change of \(S\) over time.
  • \(D\) is the diffusion coefficient.
  • \(\nabla^2S\) measures how the concentration differs from neighboring locations.
  • \(K\) controls the degradation rate.
  • \(\gamma\) is a scaling parameter related to wing size.

Biological Interpretation

The balance between diffusion and degradation determines

  • how far the morphogen spreads;
  • how long it remains present;
  • the shape of the resulting concentration field.

Gene-Product Activation

The gene-product concentration \(g\) evolves according to

\[ \frac{\partial g}{\partial t} = \gamma \left( k_1S + \frac{k_2g^2}{1+g^2} - k_3g \right). \]

This equation combines three competing processes:

  • Morphogen activation (\(k_1S\)), which increases gene-product production when morphogen concentration is high.
  • Self-activation \(\left(\frac{k_2g^2}{1+g^2}\right)\), which allows existing gene product to stimulate further production.
  • Degradation (\(-k_3g\)), which removes gene product over time.

Terms

  • \(g\) is the gene-product concentration.
  • \(\frac{\partial g}{\partial t}\) is the rate of change of \(g\) over time.
  • \(S\) is the local morphogen concentration.
  • \(k_1\) controls morphogen-driven activation.
  • \(k_2\) controls the strength of self-activation.
  • \(k_3\) controls the degradation rate.
  • \(\gamma\) scales the overall speed of the system.

Nonlinear Self-Activation

The self-activation term is

\[ \frac{k_2g^2}{1+g^2}. \]

Its behavior has three important features:

  • Nonlinear means the activation does not increase at a constant rate as \(g\) increases.
  • Self-activation means existing gene product promotes the production of more gene product.
  • The denominator \(1+g^2\) limits the activation at high concentrations, preventing unbounded growth.

Biological Interpretation

Together, self-activation and degradation create a biological switch:

  • Below a critical morphogen concentration, \(g\) returns to zero.
  • Above the threshold, \(g\) stabilizes at a positive value.
  • Cells with a stable positive value of \(g\) later become pigmented.

Boundary Conditions

The model assumes that morphogen cannot diffuse across

  • the outer edge of the wing;
  • wing veins.

This is expressed by the zero-flux boundary condition

\[ \frac{\partial S}{\partial \mathbf{n}} = 0 \qquad \text{on } \partial\Omega. \]

where

  • \(S\) is the morphogen concentration.
  • \(\frac{\partial S}{\partial \mathbf{n}}\) is the rate at which the morphogen changes in the direction perpendicular to the boundary.
  • \(\mathbf{n}\) is the outward normal vector, a vector pointing directly away from the boundary.
  • \(\partial\Omega\) denotes the boundary of the computational domain.

Numerical Method

Finite Differences

  • The continuous wing is replaced by a finite grid.
  • Spatial derivatives are approximated using finite differences.
  • The Laplacian is computed with a second-order central-difference stencil.

Ghost Nodes

  • Ghost nodes enforce the zero-flux boundary condition.
  • Artificial boundary values are chosen so that the normal derivative is zero.
  • This prevents morphogen from leaving the computational domain.

Time Integration

  • Time evolution is computed using the forward Euler method.
  • The emphasis is on reproducing qualitative biological patterns rather than high numerical accuracy.

Main Results

Reproducing Cautery Experiments

The simulations reproduce Murray’s cauterization experiments, in which small holes are burned into developing butterfly wings.

The model predicts that

  • holes placed near the morphogen source interrupt pigment-band formation;
  • holes farther from the source allow pigment bands to develop before diffusion is disrupted.

These results support the idea that pigment patterns depend on the movement of a diffusing morphogen rather than a fixed developmental blueprint.

Effect of Scale

The parameter \(\gamma\) changes the effective wing size without changing the dimensions of the computational grid.

As \(\gamma\) increases,

  • the activated region occupies a smaller fraction of the wing;
  • pigment bands become more localized.

This demonstrates that the same mathematical model can generate different patterns simply by changing the scale of the domain.

Constructing a Wing-Shaped Domain

Rather than solving the equations on a simple square, the author constructs a butterfly wing by

  • selecting boundary points;
  • interpolating them with Lagrange polynomials;
  • embedding the resulting outline in a square computational grid.

This allows the reaction–diffusion model to be solved on a domain that more closely resembles a real butterfly wing.

Multiple Morphogens

The report also explores multiple interacting morphogen systems.

The simulations

  • evolve two morphogen fields simultaneously;
  • produce distinct gene-product distributions;
  • generate more complex pigmentation patterns than a single morphogen system.

This suggests that multiple developmental signals may help explain the diversity of butterfly wing patterns observed in nature.

Strengths

  • Converts Murray’s theoretical model into a numerical simulation.
  • Clearly explains the governing equations.
  • Clearly explains the boundary conditions.
  • Clearly explains the numerical implementation.
  • Uses a wing-shaped computational domain rather than a simple rectangle.
  • Demonstrates how parameter changes alter biological patterns.
  • Bridges mathematical theory and computational experimentation.

Limitations

  • Treats the wing as a largely homogeneous domain.
  • Does not explicitly model many structural features of real butterfly wings.
  • Represents geometry indirectly through a finite-difference grid.
  • A graph-based or irregular-mesh representation may better preserve wing veins and compartment boundaries.

Questions

  • How sensitive are the simulated patterns to grid resolution?
  • Would a higher-order or implicit time-stepping method change the results?
  • Should diffusion coefficients vary across veins or wing compartments?
  • Could wing boundaries be extracted directly from photographs?
  • Could the graph Laplacian replace the finite-difference Laplacian?
  • How should multiple morphogens be coupled?
  • How can simulated gene-product fields be compared quantitatively with observed pigmentation?

Influence on My Work

This report makes the transition from theory to implementation concrete.

It demonstrates that Murray’s model can be simulated on an idealized butterfly wing using finite differences.

My project may instead

  • extract wing geometry directly from photographs;
  • represent the wing as a graph;
  • simulate diffusion using the graph Laplacian;
  • compare simulated fields with observed butterfly wing patterns.

A graph-based approach may provide

  • a more faithful representation of irregular geometry;
  • explicit treatment of veins and wing compartments;
  • a direct connection between measured wing structure and computation;
  • quantitative comparison between simulations and real butterfly wings.

Vocabulary

  • Morphogen — A signaling molecule that diffuses through developing tissue and provides positional information to surrounding cells.

  • Gene product — The molecule produced when a gene is expressed. In this model, its concentration determines whether a cell ultimately becomes pigmented.

  • Self-activation — A positive feedback mechanism in which existing gene product stimulates the production of more gene product.

  • Nonlinear — A relationship in which the output is not directly proportional to the input. Doubling the input does not necessarily double the response.

  • Zero-flux boundary condition — A boundary condition that prevents morphogen from crossing the edge of the computational domain.

  • Normal vector — A vector that points perpendicular to a surface or boundary. It is used to describe diffusion across the boundary.

  • Computational domain — The region over which the equations are solved. In this report, the domain is a butterfly-wing-shaped region embedded in a square grid.

  • Finite-difference method — A numerical technique that approximates derivatives using values at neighboring grid points.

  • Central-difference stencil — A finite-difference formula that estimates a derivative by using values on both sides of a point.

  • Ghost node — An artificial grid point outside the computational domain used to enforce boundary conditions.

  • Forward Euler method — A simple numerical method that advances the solution forward in time using the current rate of change.

  • Grid resolution — The spacing between grid points in a numerical simulation. Finer grids generally produce more accurate approximations but require more computation.

  • Lagrange interpolation — A polynomial interpolation method used in the report to construct a smooth butterfly-wing boundary from selected points.

  • Computational grid — The collection of discrete points on which the differential equations are approximated and solved.
